title: Externalities & Pollution
description: When markets ignore environmental damage — internalizing the cost

concepts.title: Pollution as Externality
concepts.contentHtml:
Pollution is the textbook negative externality. A power plant emits sulfur dioxide that causes acid rain. A factory discharges waste into a river. A truck emits CO₂ contributing to climate change.

In each case, the polluter doesn't bear the full cost. Damage falls on neighbors, downstream communities, future generations. Private cost is below social cost. Output is too high; pollution is too high.

This isn't moral failure on the polluter's part — it's a structural feature of markets. Without a mechanism to make polluters pay, individually rational decisions produce collectively irrational outcomes.

Environmental economics is largely about designing those mechanisms.

concepts.title: Optimal Pollution Isn't Zero
concepts.contentHtml:
A surprising result for non-economists: the optimal level of pollution isn't zero.

Logic: nearly all economic activity produces some pollution. Eliminating pollution entirely requires eliminating the activity entirely — at huge cost.

The optimum: where the marginal social cost of additional pollution equals the marginal social benefit of the activity producing it. Below that level, the value of more activity exceeds its incremental harm. Above it, the harm exceeds the value.

Implication: cost-benefit thinking applies to environmental policy. We should reduce pollution to where the next ton of abatement costs more than the damage it prevents.

This framing is uncomfortable to some environmentalists who see any pollution as wrong. But the alternative — pretend zero pollution is achievable — leads to bad policy. The honest question is how to get the costs and benefits right.

concepts.title: Quantity vs Price Instruments
concepts.contentHtml:
Two main approaches to internalize pollution costs.

Price instruments (Pigouvian taxes): set a tax per unit of pollution. Polluters reduce up to where marginal abatement cost equals the tax. Quantity is determined by market response.

Quantity instruments (cap-and-trade): set a cap on total pollution. Issue tradable permits up to that level. Permit price is determined by market clearing.

Under certainty, the two are equivalent (Weitzman 1974). The cap-and-trade permit price equals the optimal Pigouvian tax.

Under uncertainty, they differ. If the marginal damage curve is steep (each additional ton matters a lot), quantity instruments are better — you cap at the right level even if costs are uncertain. If marginal damages are flatter but abatement costs are steep, price instruments are better.

For climate change, this debate matters. Climate damages are highly uncertain; abatement costs are too. Both instruments have advocates.

concepts.title: Command-and-Control vs Market-Based
concepts.contentHtml:
The historical alternative to economic instruments: command-and-control regulation. Specific rules: this technology must be used; that emission rate is the maximum; this product is banned.

Examples: catalytic converters mandated on cars; CFC refrigerants banned; specific pollution limits per source.

Command-and-control is politically simpler (no taxes to oppose) and ensures specific outcomes. Drawbacks:

– Inflexibility — same rules apply to all sources, even when costs vary.

– No incentive to reduce below the limit.

– Slow innovation — once technology meets the rule, no incentive to do better.

– Politically captured — regulated industries often shape the rules to favor incumbents.

Market-based instruments (taxes, permits) achieve given environmental outcomes at lower total cost. Empirical comparisons in US sulfur dioxide regulation (the SO₂ trading system 1995-2005) showed cost savings of 30-50% relative to command-and-control alternatives.

Most economists prefer market-based approaches for these efficiency reasons. Politics often pushes the other way.

concepts.title: The Broader Environmental Picture
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond air pollution, environmental economics covers:

Water pollution and quality: upstream pollution affects downstream users. Trading systems for water rights and pollution permits exist in some places (Murray-Darling in Australia, US TMDL programs).

Biodiversity loss: hard to price because non-market values dominate. Polices include protected areas, payments for ecosystem services, biodiversity offsetting.

Plastics and waste: producer responsibility schemes, deposit-refund systems, landfill levies.

Land use and habitat: protected areas, conservation easements, agricultural set-asides.

Resource depletion: sustainable yield management for fisheries, forestry, groundwater.

The unifying theme: real-world markets ignore environmental costs. Without policy intervention, environmental quality declines. The right design of intervention varies by context — but the basic case for some intervention is robust.

title: Cap-and-Trade vs Carbon Tax
description: Quantity vs price instruments, Weitzman's rule, real-world emissions trading systems

concepts.title: How Cap-and-Trade Works
concepts.contentHtml:
The government caps total emissions at some level. It then creates that many permits — each allowing one ton of CO₂ (or other pollutant). Permits are distributed (auctioned, given freely, or mixed).

Polluters must hold permits equal to their emissions. They can buy more if they need to, sell if they have extras.

Result: a market for permits emerges. Firms that can abate cheaply do so and sell their unused permits. Firms that find abatement expensive buy permits instead. Total abatement happens at the lowest possible cost.

The mechanism delivers a target environmental outcome (the cap) with minimum total cost. The price emerges endogenously from market trading.

concepts.title: EU Emissions Trading System
concepts.contentHtml:
The world's largest carbon market: the EU ETS, launched 2005. Covers ~40% of EU emissions across power, industry, and aviation.

Phases 1 and 2 (2005-2012) had problems: too many free allocations, over-supply, low and volatile permit prices. Over-allocation crashed Phase 1 prices to near zero by 2007, and the 2008 financial crisis pushed Phase 2 prices down to roughly €8-15.

Phase 3 reforms (2013+) tightened the cap, moved more allocations to auction. Phase 4 (2021+) accelerated the cap reduction.

By 2023-24, EU ETS prices were roughly €60-100/ton — high enough to drive substantial coal-to-gas switching, renewable investment, and industrial efficiency.

The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM, phasing in 2023-26) extends ETS pricing to imports — addressing 'carbon leakage' where domestic firms move production to less-regulated jurisdictions.

concepts.title: Carbon Taxes
concepts.contentHtml:
Sweden introduced a carbon tax in 1991. Currently $130+/ton — among the world's highest. Sweden has cut emissions ~30% since 1990 while GDP grew ~80% — a rough decoupling.

Other carbon-tax countries: Finland, Norway, Switzerland, France, Canada (industrial pricing; its consumer fuel charge was scrapped in 2025), Japan (small), South Africa, Singapore, Argentina.

British Columbia introduced one in 2008 (C$10/ton initially, C$80/ton by 2024) with revenue recycled through income-tax cuts. Emissions fell ~10% in the affected sectors with no measurable economic harm. Even so, BC scrapped the consumer tax in 2025, a sign of how politically fragile visible carbon prices are.

The 'revenue recycling' design — using carbon-tax revenue to cut other taxes (income, payroll) or to fund per-capita 'carbon dividends' — addresses the regressive burden and improves political acceptability.

The US has resisted federal carbon taxes despite repeated proposals. Some states (California) have cap-and-trade; Washington has a cap-and-invest program; the federal Inflation Reduction Act (2022) subsidized clean tech rather than pricing carbon, and many of its credits were cut back in 2025.

concepts.title: Hybrid Designs
concepts.contentHtml:
The cleanest theoretical distinction (price vs quantity) blurs in practice. Most real systems use hybrids.

Price floors and ceilings in cap-and-trade: California's program has a price floor (auction reserve) and a 'price ceiling' that releases permits if prices spike. This bounds the price uncertainty inherent in pure quantity instruments.

Quantity safety valves in carbon taxes: rare but possible — adjust the tax rate based on emission outcomes.

Banking and borrowing: permits can be saved for future use (banking) or used early in exchange for future quotas (borrowing). Smooths price volatility.

Sectoral exemptions and floors: protect trade-exposed industries from competitive disadvantage.

The result: real cap-and-trade systems aren't pure quantity instruments, and real carbon taxes have flexibility built in. The clean choice between Weitzman's two instruments is largely theoretical.

concepts.title: Political Economy
concepts.contentHtml:
Why has carbon pricing spread less than economists hoped?

Visibility. Taxes and visible permit prices are politically vulnerable. Hidden costs (regulation, subsidies) hide more easily.

Distributional concerns. Without revenue recycling, carbon prices fall heavily on poorer households. France's 2018 yellow-vest protests against fuel taxes are the cautionary tale.

Industry opposition. Concentrated industry interests (fossil fuels, energy-intensive manufacturing) lobby aggressively against pricing while diffuse benefits (cleaner air, climate stability) lack constituencies.

International coordination problem. Climate is a global problem; pricing is national. Countries that act unilaterally fear losing competitive position.

Despite these obstacles, carbon pricing has expanded. By 2024, ~25% of global emissions are covered by some form of carbon pricing. Average prices remain too low for ambitious climate targets, but the institutional foundations are spreading. The next decade will determine whether carbon prices reach the levels needed to meaningfully constrain emissions.

title: Common-Pool Resources
description: Tragedy of the commons, Ostrom's design principles, fisheries, aquifers

concepts.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
concepts.contentHtml:
Garrett Hardin's 1968 essay framed a classic problem. Imagine a pasture open to all herders. Each adds animals to maximize private gain — each extra animal yields full benefit but only spreads degradation cost across all users.

The result: tragedy of the commons. Each user has individual incentive to over-graze; collectively, the pasture is destroyed.

The pattern recurs: overfishing, aquifer depletion, deforestation, atmospheric carbon, antibiotic overuse, traffic congestion.

Hardin's prescribed solutions: privatization (assign property rights so users bear full cost) or government regulation (impose limits).

The framing was influential, but Elinor Ostrom showed it was incomplete. There's a third option Hardin missed: community self-governance.

concepts.title: Ostrom's Insight
concepts.contentHtml:
Elinor Ostrom (Nobel 2009) studied actual commons management around the world: Swiss alpine pastures, Japanese village forests, Spanish irrigation systems, Maine lobster fisheries, Nepalese forests.

What she found: many commons aren't tragic. Communities have managed shared resources sustainably for centuries through informal rules and self-governance.

The conditions for success aren't accidental. Ostrom identified a pattern of features in successful commons management — what became known as her design principles.

The key implication: state ownership and privatization aren't the only choices. Local communities, given the right structure, can manage commons effectively. Top-down imposition of property rights has often destroyed functioning local management.

concepts.title: Ostrom's Design Principles
concepts.contentHtml:
Eight conditions for successful commons management:

1. Clear boundaries. Who is in the user community; what resource is being managed.

2. Rules match local conditions. Rules tailored to ecology and social context — not imposed templates.

3. Collective choice arrangements. Users participate in modifying the rules.

4. Monitoring. Either users monitor themselves or hire monitors accountable to users.

5. Graduated sanctions. Violations penalized in proportion to severity, with first-offense leniency.

6. Conflict resolution. Cheap, accessible mechanisms to resolve disputes.

7. Right to organize. External authorities recognize the community's right to govern.

8. Nested structures for larger commons (rules layered across local-regional-national levels).

These aren't a recipe — successful commons exhibit them in different ways. The principles describe what well-functioning systems share, not a checklist for designing new ones.

concepts.title: Fisheries and Their Failure
concepts.contentHtml:
Open-ocean fisheries are the textbook tragedy. Many global fisheries are overexploited or collapsed.

The Atlantic cod fishery off Newfoundland collapsed in 1992 after sustained overfishing. The cod biomass remains depressed three decades later — recovery has been slow and incomplete.

Solutions vary in effectiveness:

Catch quotas (total allowable catch divided among users): reduce overfishing but create racing — fishermen rush to catch before quota is exhausted.

Individual transferable quotas (ITQs): assign each fisherman a tradable share of the total catch. Iceland's move to vessel quotas in 1984, then a full ITQ system in 1990, stabilized its fisheries. Now widely used.

Marine protected areas: ban fishing in sensitive areas. Allows replenishment.

Co-management: Maine lobster fishery's complex local rules and quotas — a real-world Ostrom-style success.

The successes share: well-defined property rights or use rules, monitoring, and enforceable limits. The failures share: open access, weak enforcement, political capture by short-term-interested fishermen.

concepts.title: Climate as Global Commons
concepts.contentHtml:
The atmosphere is the largest commons. CO₂ emissions anywhere affect climate everywhere. No country has individual incentive to fully internalize the global cost.

This is why climate policy has been so hard. Every Ostrom design principle is hard to satisfy at global scale:

– Boundaries: who's in the agreement, who's out (developing vs developed countries).

– Local rules: hard to negotiate global rules that work for diverse country circumstances.

– Monitoring: emissions are observable but verification is contentious.

– Sanctions: no global authority to enforce.

– Conflict resolution: diplomacy is slow and weak.

The Kyoto Protocol (1997) attempted top-down quotas but excluded major emitters and lacked enforcement. The Paris Agreement (2015) pivoted to bottom-up Nationally Determined Contributions — countries set their own targets, with periodic ratcheting up. More inclusive, but weaker on enforcement.

Whether the Paris approach can deliver the 1.5°C or 2°C targets remains uncertain. Most analysts believe current pledges put the world on a 2.5-3°C trajectory. The commons problem at global scale remains genuinely unsolved.

title: Discounting the Future
description: Social discount rate, Stern vs Nordhaus, intergenerational ethics

concepts.title: The Discounting Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Climate damages largely fall on future generations. Climate mitigation requires costs today.

To compare them, you need a discount rate: how much you weight a dollar of damage in 2100 vs a dollar of cost in 2025.

Tiny changes in the rate produce huge differences in present-value calculations over century-long horizons.

At a 1% discount rate, $100 of damage in 100 years is worth $37 today.

At 5%, it's $0.76.

At 7%, it's $0.12.

The same future damage is 300 times more present-day-relevant under a 1% rate than a 7% rate. This single parameter drives most of the disagreement over climate cost-benefit analysis.

concepts.title: Two Components of Discounting
concepts.contentHtml:
The Ramsey formula: r = δ + η·g.

δ (pure rate of time preference): how much you discount future simply because it's future. Often interpreted as ethical question — should we weight future lives less than current ones?

η (elasticity of marginal utility): how much an extra dollar matters more to a poor person than a rich one. Future generations may be richer; their marginal dollar matters less.

g (growth rate of consumption): rate at which future people will be richer.

Even with δ = 0 (treating future generations as equal in principle), if g is positive and η is positive, future damages get discounted because future people are richer.

concepts.title: Stern vs Nordhaus
concepts.contentHtml:
The Stern Review (2006) used δ = 0.1% (essentially zero pure time preference) and concluded climate change required immediate, aggressive action — costs of inaction far exceeded costs of action.

William Nordhaus (Nobel 2018) argued for δ = 1.5% — closer to observed market rates — implying more gradual action.

Stern's argument: ethical. We shouldn't weight future lives less just because they're future. Discrimination by birth date is no more justified than discrimination by race or sex.

Nordhaus's argument: descriptive. Real markets discount the future. People prefer current consumption. Economic models should reflect actual preferences, not impose ethical positions.

Both have a point. Pure-ethical discounting may be too low to capture real preference for present consumption. But pure market rates may inappropriately downweight future generations who can't trade in current markets.

The compromise emerging: 'declining discount rates' that start moderate and fall to lower values for very-long horizons. The UK Treasury's official discount rate uses this approach.

concepts.title: Social Cost of Carbon
concepts.contentHtml:
The social cost of carbon (SCC) is the present value of damages from emitting one additional ton of CO₂.

Estimates vary enormously based on assumptions:

– Nordhaus's DICE model with traditional discounting: ~$50/ton.

– Stern-style low discounting: $200-400/ton.

– EPA estimates (proposed 2022, finalized 2023): ~$190/ton, accounting for tail risks and updated science; the US federal government stopped using them in 2025.

– IMF and academic estimates including catastrophic risk: $200-1000/ton.

The SCC matters because it underlies cost-benefit analysis of climate policy. A higher SCC justifies more aggressive mitigation; a lower one less.

Real-world carbon prices are mostly well below recent SCC estimates. Even high prices like the EU ETS are at the low end of the SCC range. This implies most jurisdictions are under-pricing carbon — not over-regulating.

concepts.title: Intergenerational Ethics
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond technical economics, climate policy raises ethical questions that economic models can't fully answer.

Standing: do future generations have moral standing equal to current ones? If so, what discount rate is consistent with that?

Catastrophic risks: standard expected-value analysis may understate the value of preventing tail risks. The expected damage from ordinary climate change may be $X; the expected damage from a 5% probability of civilizational collapse is also $X, but morally distinct.

Intergenerational coordination: we can't bargain with the future. Markets don't represent unborn generations. Some form of stewardship beyond pure preference satisfaction may be needed.

Sustainability: some argue current consumption shouldn't deplete capacity for future production. Hartwick's rule and 'strong sustainability' frameworks try to formalize this.

Economists tend toward technical approaches; philosophers toward ethical ones; both are necessary. The honest framing: discount rate choice is partly empirical (what real preferences are) and partly normative (what they should be). Economic analysis can quantify; it can't decide.

title: Climate Economics
description: Integrated assessment models, social cost of carbon, abatement curves

concepts.title: Integrated Assessment Models
concepts.contentHtml:
Integrated assessment models (IAMs) couple climate science and economics in single frameworks.

The basic structure:

1. An economic model produces emissions as a function of activity.

2. A simplified climate model translates emissions to temperature change.

3. A damage function maps temperature change to economic damages.

4. A welfare criterion (often discounted utility) is maximized over policy choices.

The output: optimal carbon prices, emission paths, temperature trajectories, welfare costs.

The leading IAMs: DICE (Nordhaus), FUND (Tol), PAGE (Hope). They differ in calibration, damage functions, and policy treatments.

IAMs are simplifications — vastly more abstract than serious climate models. Their value is integration: forcing economic and climate calculations into a single framework rather than reasoning separately.

concepts.title: Damage Functions
concepts.contentHtml:
The most contested element of IAMs is the damage function — how much economic damage does each degree of warming cause?

Nordhaus's DICE damage function: ~2% of GDP loss at 3°C, ~10% at 6°C. Quadratic in temperature.

Critics (Burke-Hsiang-Miguel, Weitzman, Stern) argue damages are systematically understated:

– Standard models assume smooth damages; reality includes tipping points.

– Effects on labor productivity, agriculture, and migration are likely larger than current estimates.

– Damages from non-market values (biodiversity, indigenous cultures, mental health) are excluded.

– Tail risks (5°C+ scenarios with civilizational disruption) get under-weighted in expected-value calculations.

Updated damage functions (Burke-Hsiang-Miguel 2015; Bilal-Känzig 2024) suggest damages 5-10× higher than older estimates. The implications for optimal policy: much steeper carbon prices, much faster mitigation.

concepts.title: Marginal Abatement Cost Curves
concepts.contentHtml:
How much does it cost to reduce emissions?

Marginal abatement cost (MAC) curves stack abatement opportunities by cost. Cheap measures (energy efficiency, low-cost renewables) sit on the left; expensive ones (carbon capture, exotic geo-engineering) on the right.

McKinsey's famous MAC curves show many low-cost or even cost-saving abatement opportunities exist — energy efficiency, modern lighting, building retrofits. Why aren't they already being implemented? Market failures: principal-agent problems (landlords vs tenants), information costs, capital constraints, behavioral barriers.

The 'low-hanging fruit' on MAC curves implies much abatement is cheap or free. But getting it implemented requires more than carbon prices — it requires removing the specific barriers that block private investment.

Even after exhausting cheap abatement, deeper decarbonization (heavy industry, aviation, shipping) requires more expensive technology. MAC curves help quantify how much we should invest in R&D to bring expensive technologies down the curve.

concepts.title: Decarbonization Pathways
concepts.contentHtml:
Net-zero by 2050 is now the headline target for most major economies. What does it require?

Power sector: ~80-90% renewable + nuclear + storage. Already partly there in some countries (UK power was over 50% low-carbon in 2024).

Transport: electrification of cars, trucks, buses. EVs reaching ~20% of new sales globally by 2024, faster in China and Europe. Aviation and shipping decarbonization remains difficult.

Heating: heat pumps replacing gas furnaces in buildings. Slow uptake in many markets.

Industry: hardest. Steel, cement, chemicals, fertilizer all use processes that aren't easy to electrify. Hydrogen and carbon capture loom large here.

Agriculture: reducing methane (cattle), N₂O (fertilizer), and land-use change. Hardest to abate in absolute terms.

Negative emissions: some IAMs require large-scale removal (BECCS, direct air capture) to balance hard-to-abate emissions.

Each pathway has different costs and feasibility. The economics literature is shifting from 'is decarbonization cost-effective' (yes) to 'how do we get there given political and technological constraints' (much harder).

concepts.title: Adaptation
concepts.contentHtml:
Even with aggressive mitigation, some warming is locked in. Adaptation — reducing damages from a warmer world — is part of climate policy.

Examples: sea walls, drought-resistant crops, heat-tolerant building designs, water management, early-warning systems, climate-relevant insurance.

Adaptation is partly local — each region faces different impacts. It's also partly market-driven: private actors adapt as costs become apparent, sometimes (as in coastal real estate markets) earlier than policy.

Mitigation vs adaptation tradeoff: mitigation is global (any country's emissions affect everyone) but expensive; adaptation is local (each country chooses its own level) but doesn't reduce the underlying problem.

The economic case: invest in mitigation up to the point where marginal cost exceeds marginal future damage; invest in adaptation up to the point where marginal cost exceeds marginal damage prevention.

Empirically: most analysis suggests we're substantially under-investing in both. The political economy of climate policy makes neither easy.

The 21st century may be defined by how well humanity manages this dual challenge. The economics is reasonably clear; the politics is harder.
